subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Tie Guan Yin
description: A 60-second lesson on Tie Guan Yin.

hook.text: Tie Guan Yin (Iron Goddess of Mercy) is China's most famous oolong, named after a Buddhist deity.

buildup.text: Grown in Fujian's Anxi county, it's tightly rolled into small, dense pellets that unfurl when brewed.

discovery.text: Traditional Tie Guan Yin is charcoal-roasted, producing a warm, honeyed sweetness with orchid aroma.

twist.text: Modern 'green' Tie Guan Yin skips heavy roasting for a lighter, more floral style—controversial among purists.

climax.text: High-quality Tie Guan Yin is steeped 7+ times using gongfu method—tiny pot, lots of leaf, short steeps.

punchline.text: A goddess's name, orchid perfume, seven infusions of wonder.

quiz.question: What is in the name 'Tie Guan Yin'?
options: Iron Goddess of Mercy—a Buddhist deity

details.summary: Tie Guan Yin, or Iron Goddess of Mercy, is China's most famous oolong tea from Anxi, Fujian. Modern light-roast versions are floral and buttery with jade-green leaves, while traditional roasted versions offer toasty depth. It is one of the most consumed specialty teas globally.
details.whyItMatters: Tie Guan Yin introduced millions of people to oolong tea. The tension between modern light and traditional roasted styles reflects broader debates about authenticity in tea culture.
takeaways: Tie Guan Yin is China's most famous oolong from Fujian
Modern versions are light and floral; traditional are roasted
It is tightly rolled into small balls that unfurl when brewed

faq.question: What does Tie Guan Yin taste like?
faq.answer: Light-roast versions taste of orchid, butter, and fresh cream with a smooth, sweet finish. Traditional roasted versions have toasty, caramel, and dried fruit notes with more body. Both share a distinctive mineral quality and a lingering aftertaste called huigan in Chinese.

faq.question: How is Tie Guan Yin different from other oolongs?
faq.answer: Its unique cultivar produces a distinctive orchid fragrance that other varieties cannot replicate. The tight ball-rolling technique is characteristic of Anxi oolongs. Multiple roasting passes in traditional production develop a layered complexity that sets it apart from lighter styles.
